paras: The lynching of Winn at Ivanpah was the hanging of an Indian man by four masked men at the mining camp of Ivanpah, San Bernardino County, California, in March 1881. Winn was accused of shooting dead Daniel Keistler, or Kestler, a stock-raiser, and other Indians had caught him and handed him over before the masked men took him out at night. A San Francisco wire carried the story across the country, often under headlines that made a joke of the victim being an Indian.

According to an account first printed in a San Bernardino paper, the trouble began on a Tuesday or Wednesday in mid-March, when Winn threw a woman into a well at Ivanpah; she climbed out with slight bruises. Fearing that the whites would kill him, the account says, he went to Kestler's ranch "for some old grudge" and shot Kestler several times, then locked the body in the cabin. The San Francisco wire instead put the killing down to "some trifling difficulty" and called Winn only "a renegade Indian."

Two Indians who had been with Winn went to Ivanpah and told the whites and Indians there, and a party went down to the cabin, caught Winn, tied him and brought him back to town. Hiram Clark and a man named Brookfield went down to Kestler's to check the story, while the Indians held Winn in Clark's saloon. Late in the evening, as miners sat talking and drinking, four masked men entered, ordered the crowd to stand back, took Winn out and hanged him from a butcher's gallows nearby.

When the miners went to look for him, they found him hanging, with one masked man guarding the body while the other three dug a grave. The guard told them to "take a walk," and they went back to the saloon. The local account added that Winn had confessed to killing three other white men and four Indians, among them his own child, and that the Indians would have hanged him themselves had they not feared white interference.

The coverage names none of the masked men and reports no inquest, arrest or official inquiry. On 3 April the Arizona Weekly Citizen reprinted from the Prescott Miner an unconfirmed report that the Indians around Ivanpah had "gone on the war path," without connecting it to the hanging.

The fullest version appeared in the Daily Los Angeles Herald on 27 March under the headline "A DOUBLE TRAGEDY. Murder and Masked Lynchers at Ivanpak," reprinted from a San Bernardino paper, and the Pioche Weekly Record ran a shorter form credited to the San Bernardino Times. Its tone was light: it described Winn as wanting to go "to the happy hunting grounds on the square, like a good Indian" and said he "was hard to beat in a polite game."

Elsewhere the story travelled as a San Francisco dispatch of 29 March based on mail advices, which the Chicago Daily Tribune headed "HANGING A REDSKIN" and the Helena Weekly Herald "A Murderer Lynched." The Cheyenne Daily Leader titled it "Another Good Indian" and the Memphis Daily Appeal "Reformed a Bad Indian," treating the hanging as a satisfactory end. From 30 March into April the item was cut down to a sentence in news summaries in Delaware, Iowa and Minnesota, one of which said "a party of reds" had delivered the prisoner. Other condensed versions ran in the New Ulm Weekly Review and, in Wisconsin, the River Falls Journal and the Superior Times. No paper condemned the lynchers.

Accounts differ on whom Winn was taken from. The San Bernardino account says the Indians held him in a saloon and names no officer, while the wire says Indians "delivered the murderer to the authorities" and some briefs said he was "taken from jail." The local account is the closest and most detailed source; the jail version appears only in one-sentence summaries.

reader.title: Lynching of Winn at Ivanpah
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Four masked men took an Indian accused of murder from the men holding him and hanged him (A1, A13); the wire says masked men took him from the authorities and hung him (A2, A7).

Every account says masked men hanged the Indian without any legal process (A1, A2, A3); the local account counts four of them (A1, A13), and the hanging punished his alleged killing of Kestler (A1, A2). The victim is described as an Indian, not as Black (A1, A2), so the case falls outside anti-Black violence.

The San Bernardino account (A1, A13) and the San Francisco wire from mail advices (A2, A7) agree on the killing of Kestler/Keistler by an Indian, his capture by other Indians, and his hanging by masked men, though they differ on details, which suggests separate sourcing.
